post.caption: This ruby was grown in a flame. At 17, French chemist Auguste Verneuil became Edmond Frémy's assistant. He lodged sealed notes in 1891, then announced the method in 1902. Powder falls through an oxygen and hydrogen flame, about 2,000 degrees Celsius. The powder melts and builds up as a crystal called a boule. A little chromium mixed into the powder makes it red. It is corundum, the same mineral as natural ruby, and curved growth lines and gas bubbles help gemologists spot it. Flame fusion is still a common way to make synthetic ruby, and tiny synthetic rubies also serve as bearings inside watches.
